records.sourceFile: The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Veen J, Bergh C, Cao Y, Randers MB, Krustrup P, Edholm P. The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2026;36:e70202.
paper.abstract: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 10 controlled trials of cold-water immersion after match or simulated match play in competitive soccer players, measuring sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24 to 72 hours. CWI improved strength, jump, creatine kinase and soreness recovery but not sprint, and all prediction intervals included no effect.
paper.tldr: After soccer match play, cold-water immersion improved recovery of maximal strength, lowered creatine kinase and reduced soreness compared with passive rest, with a small jump gain seen only at 48 hours. It did not improve sprint recovery, and the prediction intervals are wide enough to include no effect.
paper.methods: PRISMA review (PROSPERO CRD42024543581) searching PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus and SPORTDiscus in January 2024 and January 2025 for RCTs of competitive male or female soccer players aged 15 to 45 given CWI (5-20 min at 5-15 C) or passive or placebo control after a match, simulated match or similar activity. Outcomes were 20 m sprint, countermovement jump, maximal voluntary contraction, creatine kinase and soreness at 24, 48 or 72 h; quality was rated with PEDro and data pooled as SMDs with 95% CIs and prediction intervals (DerSimonian-Laird random effects, Stata 18.5).
paper.findings: Compared with passive rest, CWI improved MVC recovery overall (SMD 1.02), with effects at 24 h (SMD 1.22), 48 h (SMD 1.10, 95% CI -0.02 to 2.21, p = 0.05) and 72 h (SMD 0.65), and lowered CK at all three time points (overall SMD -0.77). CMJ improved overall (SMD 0.38) but only at 48 h (SMD 0.53), soreness was lower at 24 h and 72 h (overall SMD -1.04) but not at 48 h, and 20 m sprint was unaffected at any time point. The prediction intervals for all outcomes included no effect.
paper.limitations: Blinding of participants and researchers is impossible with CWI, and no included trial blinded participants or therapists; samples were small (8 to 43 per trial). Publication bias was assessed only qualitatively, the 72 h soreness result rests on one study, and only one trial included female players (9 of 22). The 48 h MVC effect is called significant although its 95% CI crosses zero.
paper.practicalImplications: Post-match CWI (8-15 C for 5-15 min in these trials) may help soccer players recover strength and reduce soreness and creatine kinase over the next three days. It showed no sprint benefit, and the wide prediction intervals mean the effect in a given team may be small or absent.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can consider CWI as one post-match recovery tool for strength and soreness, not as a sprint-recovery tool. The jump benefit appeared only at the 48 h test, so a jump test the day after a match may not show it.
paper.rtp: Relevant to recovery after match play in players who are not injured. The review does not study injured players or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform clearance or rehabilitation loading.
